content: Past perfect = had + past participle.
It marks the past BEFORE the past.
Two past moments, one of them earlier:
"When the investigation began, the
thief had already gone."
The plain past sets the scene; had +
done reaches further back.
"The room was empty; she had left."
Her leaving came first.
It shows which action came first.
Many languages mark this step back
with a special tense; English just
puts had before the past participle.
After, before and by the time put two
past events in order.
The event that happened FIRST takes
the past perfect (had done); the other
takes the plain past.
"After the guests had left, we sat
down to eat." (they left first)
"By the time we arrived, the show had
started." (it started first)
Many languages leave both verbs in the
plain past and let the order word do
the work; English also steps the first
verb back into had + done.
After one verb, a second verb must
take a shape. English has two:
-ING, the gerund:
enjoy, keep, finish, mind + doing.
"I enjoy going to the pool."
"They kept talking."
TO + verb, the infinitive:
decide, hope, want, need + to do.
"We decided to leave early."
"I hope to see you soon."
The first verb fixes the lane, not the
meaning. You learn each verb with its
shape, the way you learn a word.
A wrong lane sounds wrong to the ear:
"enjoy to read" and "decide reading"
are both off.
Many languages keep one shape after
every verb; English splits its verbs
into two camps, and the verb you pick
decides the shape of the next one.
A few verbs take BOTH lanes — but the
lane changes the meaning.
STOP:
"She stopped talking." = she ended it.
"She stopped to talk." = she paused in
order to talk.
REMEMBER:
"I remember locking it." = I recall the
act, now past.
"Remember to lock it." = do not forget
the task ahead.
TRY:
"Try asking her." = test it, and see
what happens.
"Try to ask her." = make the effort.
Some verbs take either lane with no
change. PREFER is one:
"I prefer walking" = "I prefer to walk."
Both are fine.
Many languages lean on one shape and
change the meaning with other words;
English lets the shape itself carry it.
